chunks.text: # Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) Basics Adobe Experience Manager, usually shortened to AEM, is Adobe's enterprise content management system for building websites, mobile apps and forms. It is part of the Adobe Experience Cloud and is widely used by large organisations to manage digital experiences across many sites and languages from a single platform. AEM is built on three open technologies from the Apache Software Foundation.

AEM is built on three open technologies from the Apache Software Foundation. Apache Sling provides the web framework that maps repository content to URLs and resolves each request to a script or servlet. The Java Content Repository, implemented by Apache Jackrabbit Oak, stores all content and assets in a hierarchical tree. OSGi, through Apache Felix, gives AEM a modular runtime where features are packaged as bundles that can be installed and updated independently.

Page templates define which components authors may place on a page, and editable templates let authors adjust the layout in the browser.

Server-side rendering of components commonly uses HTL, the HTML Template Language, together with Sling Models, which are Java classes that expose repository data to the template in a clean, testable way. AEM has two main run modes. The author instance is where editors create and preview content, and the publish instance is the one that serves live traffic.

# Java and the Spring Framework Spring is the most widely used framework for building enterprise Java applications. At its core is the Inversion of Control container, which creates objects and wires them together through dependency injection, so classes declare the collaborators they need instead of constructing them. This makes code easier to test, because dependencies can be replaced with mocks or stubs. Spring Boot builds on Spring to make standalone applications easy to create and run.

Boot builds on Spring to make standalone applications easy to create and run. Its best-known feature is auto-configuration: Spring Boot inspects the libraries on the classpath and the properties the developer has set, and then configures beans automatically — for example, if an embedded database driver is present, it sets up a data source without manual XML or Java configuration. Developers can always override these defaults.

A typical Spring Boot web application uses Spring MVC to expose REST endpoints: classes annotated with @RestController map HTTP requests to methods, and responses are serialised to JSON automatically. Spring Data JPA simplifies database access by generating repository implementations from interface method names.

# Machine Learning Basics Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which a model learns patterns from data instead of being programmed with explicit rules. In supervised learning, the training data is labelled with the correct answers, and the model learns to predict those labels for new inputs — for example, classifying an email as spam or not spam.

In unsupervised learning the data has no labels, and the model instead finds structure, such as grouping customers into clusters with similar behaviour. Data scientists split their data into a training set, used to fit the model, and a held-out test set, used to estimate how well the model generalises to unseen data.

This matters because of overfitting: a model that memorises the training examples, including their noise, can perform very well on the training set yet badly on new data. Techniques such as cross-validation, regularisation and simply collecting more data help to reduce overfitting.

Embeddings power semantic search: a question and a passage can be compared by the distance between their vectors, which is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation, where the most relevant passages are fetched first and then handed to a language model so its answer is grounded in real documents.
